facts.statement: Dromomeron is a genus of avemetatarsalian archosaurs meaning "running femur" that lived between 220 and 211.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Dromomeron (meaning "running femur") is a genus of lagerpetid avemetatarsalian which lived around 220 to 211.9 ± 0.7 million years ago.

facts.statement: Fossil remains, primarily hindlimbs, indicate that Dromomeron was about 1 meter long.
facts.quote: It is known from partial remains, largely from the hindlimbs, which indicate an animal with an overall length of 1 m.

facts.statement: The brain of D. gregorii features a floccular lobe of the cerebellum projecting into the semicircular canals, which are unusually large compared to other archosauromorphs.
facts.quote: The brain of D. gregorii is characterised by a floccular lobe of the cerebellum that projects within the space of the semicircular canals, which are large relative to other archosauromorphs.

facts.statement: The type species D. romeri is based on a complete left femur (GR 218) found at Hayden Quarry in Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
facts.quote: Dromomeron and the type species D. romeri are based on Ruth Hall Museum of Paleontology GR 218, a complete left femur from the Hayden Quarry at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.

facts.statement: The species name D. romeri honors the paleontologist Alfred Sherwood Romer.
facts.quote: The species name romeri honors influential 20th-century vertebrate paleontologist Alfred Sherwood Romer.

facts.statement: The species D. gregorii is named after Joseph T. Gregory and is based on a right femur found at Otis Chalk Quarry in Texas.
facts.quote: D. gregorii, named for Joseph T. Gregory, is based on TMM 31100–1306, a right femur (thigh bone) from the Otis Chalk Quarry, Colorado City Formation, (Dockum Group), near Otis Chalk, Texas.

facts.statement: The species D. gigas was described in 2016 from fossils found in the Quebrada del Barro Formation in northwestern Argentina.
facts.quote: A third species, D. gigas, was described by Martínez et al. (2016) on the basis of fossils recovered from the Norian Quebrada del Barro Formation in northwestern Argentina.

facts.statement: Dromomeron is classified in the clade Lagerpetonidae alongside the related genus Lagerpeton.
facts.quote: The bones of Dromomeron are most similar to those of the older pterosauromorph Lagerpeton, and the two animals have been classified together in a clade Lagerpetonidae.

facts.statement: Dromomeron fossils are found in Late Triassic rocks in the Southwestern United States and northwestern Argentina.
facts.quote: The genus contains species known from Late Triassic-age rocks of the Southwestern United States and northwestern Argentina.

facts.statement: The coexistence of Dromomeron with early dinosaurs like Chindesaurus suggests that dinosaurs did not immediately replace their archosaurian predecessors.
facts.quote: Finding the remains of four types of dinosaurs and dinosaur relatives (including Dromomeron itself) is noteworthy because it shows that dinosaurs did not immediately replace their dinosauromorph predecessors

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dromomeron and Tawa hallae are the same species; Christopher Bennett proposed they were conspecific, but Rodrigo Muller rejected this in 2017 due to distinct femoral differences.
facts.quote: Based on the study of the overlapping material of Dromomeron and Tawa hallae, Christopher Bennett proposed that the two taxa were conspecific, forming a single growth series of Dromomeron. However, noting prominent differences between their femurs which cannot be attributed to variation with age, Rodrigo Muller rejected this proposal in 2017.

facts.statement: Specimens of D. romeri are interpreted as juveniles, limiting knowledge of the species' adult size and morphology.
facts.quote: The known specimens of D. romeri have been interpreted as representing juvenile individuals, which limits knowledge of the species' adult morphology and size.

facts.statement: Dromomeron lived during the Norian to Rhaetian stages, approximately 227.3 to 201.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Rhaetian (227.3 to 201.4 million years ago)
